title: Restricted tangent calculus for bialgebras over a base algebra
statement:
Let $k$ be a field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field] and $R$ any commutative $k$-algebra. Let $C$ be a commutative unital $R$-bialgebra: its unital algebra maps $\Delta:C\to C\otimes_R C$ and $\varepsilon:C\to R$ satisfy coassociativity and both counit identities [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Set
$$L_C=\{v\in\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,R):v(cc')=\varepsilon(c)v(c')+v(c)\varepsilon(c')\},\qquad I=\ker\varepsilon.$$
Restriction gives an $R$-linear isomorphism $L_C\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_R(I/I^2,R)$. The maps $v\mapsto D_v=(1\otimes v)\Delta$ and $D\mapsto\varepsilon D$ are inverse $R$-linear bijections between $L_C$ and the $R$-linear derivations $D:C\to C$ satisfying $\Delta D=(1\otimes D)\Delta$. In convolution $(v*w)(c)=(v\otimes w)(\Delta c)$ one has $D_{v*w}=D_vD_w$, where this formula uses the same definition of $D_a$ for any $R$-linear functional $a$. The submodule $L_C$ is closed under $[v,w]=v*w-w*v$ and $v^{[p]}=v^{*p}$, and $D_{v^{[p]}}=D_v^p$. These operations give an $R$-bilinear alternating bracket satisfying the Jacobi identity and a restricted operation, meaning: $(av)^{[p]}=a^pv^{[p]}$, $\operatorname{ad}(v^{[p]})=\operatorname{ad}(v)^p$, and $(v+w)^{[p]}=v^{[p]}+w^{[p]}+\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}s_i(v,w)$, where $i s_i(v,w)$ is the coefficient of $t^{i-1}$ in $\operatorname{ad}(tv+w)^{p-1}(v)$ in $L_C\otimes_R R[t]$. For a bialgebra homomorphism $f:C\to C'$ the map $v\mapsto v\circ f$ from $L_{C'}$ to $L_C$ is $R$-linear and preserves bracket and $[p]$. A functional $v\in L_C$ corresponds to the augmented algebra map $c\mapsto\varepsilon(c)+\epsilon v(c)$ into $R[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$, naturally in augmented algebra maps. When $C$ is the coordinate algebra of an affine $R$-group, these are its relative tangent vectors at the identity, and the invariant-derivation operations are the relative Lie operations.

source.place: Propositions 10.28--10.29, printed pp.195--196, and paragraph before Proposition 11.36, p.223. The formulas are extended here to an arbitrary commutative base k-algebra and bialgebra; this generality is agent-supplied. proof.text: Write $\eta:R\to C$ for the structure map. Since $\varepsilon\eta=1_R$, every $c\in C$ has the unique decomposition $c=\eta\varepsilon(c)+j(c)$ with $j(c)\in I$. For $v\in L_C$, applying its product rule to $1\cdot1$ gives $v(1)=2v(1)$, hence $v(1)=0$ by subtraction, even for $p=2$. Its $R$-linearity then gives $v\eta=0$. For $x,y\in I$, the same rule gives $v(xy)=0$, so restriction annihilates $I^2$, the $R$-span of these products. Conversely, given $\lambda:I/I^2\to R$ linear, put $v_\lambda(c)=\lambda(j(c)\bmod I^2)$. The equality $j(cc')=\eta\varepsilon(c)j(c')+\eta\varepsilon(c')j(c)+j(c)j(c')$ proves its product rule after passage to $I/I^2$. Restriction and this formula are inverse, and both are $R$-linear. This proves the cotangent identification without any choice of basis or projectivity assumption.

source.place: Proposition 10.28, p.195, together with the augmentation-ideal description of tangent vectors in §10b; agent-supplied relative split-augmentation calculation

proof.text:
Use [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] to interpret $\Delta(c)=\sum c_1\otimes c_2$ as notation for a finite tensor expression, not a preferred decomposition. The maps below are induced by balanced bilinear maps, so their values are independent of that expression. The product of $C\otimes_RC$ is the one of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property], $(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$, so $\Delta(cc')=\sum c_1c'_1\otimes c_2c'_2$. For $v\in L_C$, multiplicativity of $\Delta$, the product rule for $v$, and the counit identities give
$$D_v(cc')=\sum c_1c'_1\bigl(\varepsilon(c_2)v(c'_2)+v(c_2)\varepsilon(c'_2)\bigr)=cD_v(c')+D_v(c)c'.$$
Thus $D_v$ is an $R$-linear derivation. Coassociativity gives
$$\Delta D_v(c)=\sum c_1\otimes c_2v(c_3)=(1\otimes D_v)\Delta(c),$$
so it is invariant. All expressions are equalities of maps obtained by tensoring linear maps; no assertion of tensor exactness is involved.

source.place: Proposition 10.29, pp.195–196; expansion of its converse over R, using only the bialgebra axioms

proof.text:
If $D$ is an invariant $R$-linear derivation, then $v=\varepsilon D$ satisfies
$$v(cc')=\varepsilon(c)v(c')+v(c)\varepsilon(c')$$
because $\varepsilon$ is an algebra map. Moreover
$$D=(1\otimes\varepsilon)\Delta D=(1\otimes\varepsilon)(1\otimes D)\Delta=D_{\varepsilon D}.$$
For any $R$-linear functional $a:C\to R$, not necessarily tangent, the other counit identity gives $\varepsilon D_a(c)=\sum\varepsilon(c_1)a(c_2)=a(c)$. Hence $a\mapsto D_a$ is injective on all functionals and the two maps in the item are inverse on tangent functionals and invariant derivations. Both are $R$-linear by their displayed formulas.

source.place: Proposition 10.29 proof, p.196; both inverse identities, with the counit identity also recorded for arbitrary functionals

proof.text:
For arbitrary $R$-linear functionals $a,b$, coassociativity and $R$-linearity give
$$D_aD_b(c)=\sum c_1a(c_2)b(c_3)=D_{a*b}(c).$$
Here composition means first $D_b$, then $D_a$; this fixes the order without assuming cocommutativity. The same threefold tensor calculation gives $(a*b)*d=a*(b*d)$, and the counit gives $a*\varepsilon=\varepsilon*a=a$. Thus convolution is associative and $R$-bilinear. In particular $D_{v*w-w*v}=D_vD_w-D_wD_v$, and induction on $n\ge1$, starting with $n=1$ and using the displayed composition equality for the induction step, gives $D_{v^{*n}}=D_v^n$.

source.place: Proposition 10.29, p.196, and the restricted-derivation paragraph before Proposition 11.36, p.223; agent-supplied convolution-order calculation

proof.text: Put $D=D_v$, $E=D_w$. Expanding $DE(cc')$ by the product rule gives $DE(c)c'+E(c)D(c')+D(c)E(c')+cDE(c')$; the corresponding expansion for $ED$ has the same middle terms. Subtraction proves that $[D,E]$ is a derivation. The invariance equations imply $\Delta DE=(1\otimes DE)\Delta$ and the same for $ED$, by substitution, so $[D,E]$ is invariant. Steps 3–4 therefore show $v*w-w*v\in L_C$. Bilinearity of the bracket follows from convolution bilinearity and $[v,v]=0$ by subtraction. The Jacobi identity follows by expanding $[D,[E,F]]+[E,[F,D]]+[F,[D,E]]$: each of $DEF,DFE,EFD,EDF,FDE,FED$ occurs once with each sign. Injectivity from step 3 gives Jacobi on $L_C$. These cancellations hold also in characteristic two.

source.place: Proposition 10.29 and its preceding invariant-bracket computation, pp.195–196; explicit elementary commutator cancellations

proof.text: The scalar fact needed for powers is valid over every $R$ here: [def-weil-field] implies that $i\in k$ is invertible for $0<i<p$. From the integer identity $i\binom pi=p\binom{p-1}{i-1}$, multiplication by $i^{-1}$ in $k$ gives $\binom pi=0$ in $k$ and hence in $R$. No cancellation in $R$ is needed. Similarly each $i$ has the specified inverse in $R$ given by the image of $i^{-1}\in k$; this statement remains meaningful if $R$ is the zero ring.

source.place: Proposition 10.38(a), p.205: scalar binomial cancellation, written using the field k rather than assuming the base R is a field

proof.text: Let $D=D_v$ and let $\mu:C\otimes_R C\to C$ be multiplication. Tensor maps and equality on pure tensors are supplied by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Set $U=D\otimes1$, $V=1\otimes D$. On $x\otimes y$, $UV$ and $VU$ both give $D(x)\otimes D(y)$, hence they commute. The product rule says $D\mu=\mu(U+V)$. Induction gives $D^n\mu=\mu(U+V)^n$: the case $n=0$ is the identity, and left composition by $D$ and substitution of $D\mu$ proves the next case. Apply [lem-sfb-commuting-binomial-expansion] with $F=k$ in $\operatorname{End}_R(C\otimes_R C)$, an associative unital $k$-algebra by restriction of scalars. Step 6 kills the interior coefficients at $n=p$, so $D^p\mu=\mu(U^p+V^p)$. On pure tensors this is $D^p(xy)=D^p(x)y+xD^p(y)$, proving that $D^p$ is an $R$-linear derivation. Iterating the invariance equation gives $\Delta D^p=(1\otimes D^p)\Delta$. By steps 3–4, $v^{*p}=\varepsilon D_v^p$ is tangent and $D_{v^{[p]}}=D_v^p$.

source.place: Paragraph before Proposition 11.36, p.223; agent-supplied commuting-operator proof of p-power closure, with the binomial input of Proposition 10.38(a), p.205

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-associative-jacobson-identities] with its field $F=k$ and its algebra $A=\operatorname{End}_R(C)$, again by restriction of scalars; it does not require $R$ to be a field or $C$ finite. Step 4 makes $v\mapsto D_v$ bracket- and power-preserving, and step 3 makes it injective. Its coefficientwise extension to polynomials is injective too: a polynomial maps to zero exactly when each of its finitely many coefficients does. Each coefficient of $\operatorname{ad}(tv+w)^{p-1}(v)$ belongs to $L_C$, by bracket closure and expansion of the finite iterated bracket. Division by $i$ is multiplication by the scalar from step 6. Consequently these coefficients map to the corresponding coefficients for $D_v,D_w$, so the cited Jacobson sum formula implies precisely the stated sum formula. The cited adjoint identity, applied to $D_v$ and evaluated at each $D_w$, gives $\operatorname{ad}(v^{[p]})=\operatorname{ad}(v)^p$. Finally $D_{av}=aD_v$ and $R$-linearity of $D_v$ give $(aD_v)^p=a^pD_v^p$; injectivity gives $(av)^{[p]}=a^pv^{[p]}$ for every $a\in R$, not just scalars in $k$.

source.place: Proposition 10.38(a),(b) and Definition 10.39, pp.205–206; paragraph before Proposition 11.36, p.223; coefficientwise passage to the invariant submodule over R

proof.text:
Let $f:C\to C'$ be a bialgebra map. Its algebra property and $\varepsilon'f=\varepsilon$ show directly that $v\circ f$ satisfies the augmentation product rule whenever $v\in L_{C'}$. For arbitrary functionals $a,b:C'\to R$, the coalgebra identity gives
$$((a*b)\circ f)(c)=(a\otimes b)\Delta'f(c)=(a\otimes b)(f\otimes f)\Delta(c)=((a\circ f)*(b\circ f))(c).$$
Precomposition is $R$-linear, hence preserves brackets; induction using this equality preserves convolution powers, in particular $[p]$. This proves the functoriality without asserting that the invariant derivations on different algebras can be composed with one another.

source.place: Proposition 10.29, p.196, naturality sentence, and paragraph before Proposition 11.36, p.223; agent-supplied explicit bialgebra-map calculation

proof.text: In $R[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)=R\oplus\epsilon R$, multiplication is $(r+\epsilon s)(r'+\epsilon s')=rr'+\epsilon(rs'+sr')$. Thus $c\mapsto\varepsilon(c)+\epsilon v(c)$ is multiplicative exactly when $v$ obeys the displayed augmentation product rule; it is unital and fixes $R$ because $v(1)=0$ and $v\eta=0$ from step 1. Conversely, an $R$-algebra map reducing to $\varepsilon$ has a unique $\epsilon$-coefficient $v$, which is $R$-linear and satisfies that rule. For an augmented algebra map $f$, substitution gives $(\varepsilon'+\epsilon v)f=\varepsilon+\epsilon(vf)$, proving the asserted naturality, even without a coalgebra condition. For an affine group with coordinate algebra $C$, maps into these dual numbers reducing to the identity section are, by definition, relative tangent vectors there; left invariance on functions is exactly $\Delta D=(1\otimes D)\Delta$. Accordingly the constructed bracket and pth iterate are its relative Lie operations, as in Milne's invariant-derivation definition. No smoothness hypothesis is used.
